# F02 dossier: Ground Truth Guild / Ledger (expert-graded evals for back-office AI)

**Verdict: WEAK, and closer to "dead as framed" than the gate said.** The one real gap is that nobody publishes an independent accuracy test of AI OASIS tools. But that gap is small, its natural payer (the AI vendors) has little reason to buy honest scores, and every route to "big" runs through a lane someone with far more money already holds. The idea survives only as a three-week buyer-demand test, described in section 9. Items I could not verify are marked as such. Arithmetic marked "mine" is my own estimate, not a sourced figure.

## 1. Gate zero: MHC is probably not what the brief assumes

- The federal provider registry lists **MHC AREA 6, LLC** (Riverview) and **MHC AREA 9, LLC** (Boca Raton) as home-health agencies. Both show the doing-business-as name "Choice Health at Home", a Tyler, Texas mailing address, and the same authorized official (Katrina Lanier, Secretary). Both records were updated 2026-04-17. [Area 9](https://npiregistry.cms.hhs.gov/api/?number=1245899020&version=2.1), [Area 6](https://npiregistry.cms.hhs.gov/api/?number=1932661725&version=2.1)
- Choice is a PE-backed Texas chain run by CEO David Jackson ([Trive Capital deal](https://prnewswire.com/news-releases/trive-capital-partners-with-choice-health-at-home-301358971.html)). Its Florida entry was announced in early 2026 as the purchase of Senior Nannies of Fort Lauderdale. That article does not mention MHC, Boca Raton or Riverview ([HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2026/02/choice-health-at-home-acquires-3-home-based-care-businesses-enters-new-state/)).
- Both MHC NPIs were created in 2019, years before Choice's Florida entry. The likeliest reading is that someone ran "MHC Area N" agencies in Florida and Choice absorbed them. I cannot tell whether that someone is the grandfather. No web source links "MHC Healthcare" to the Peremel family.
- The other "MHC HealthCare" entities I found do not fit: Maryland Healthcare Clinics, a specialty-clinic group founded in 1987 by Semyon Friedman ([site](https://mhcorp.com/about)), and an Arizona community health center ([search hit](https://mhchealthcare.org/?p=728)).
- **Consequences.** If the family sold to Choice, the RN and coder bench probably is not his to recruit. Choice also uses Apricot's AI-drafted OASIS forms ([HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2025/06/how-ai-tools-help-home-health-providers-dramatically-lessen-oasis-time-burden/)), so "independently" grading Apricot would be compromised. If MHC still operates, it is still a conflicted grader of any vendor it uses.
- **MyFinancialAdvice** has only 2004 coverage (a $300 advisor set-up fee, $150 annual renewal, 65 advisors) ([ThinkAdvisor](https://www.thinkadvisor.com/2004/06/01/the-playing-field-serving-the-not-so-wealthy/)) and an undated profile ([Gust](https://gust.com/companies/myfinancialadvice_inc)). Whether the advisor network is live is unverified.

**One question for the family settles most of this:** does MHC still own and operate agencies, or did it sell them, and to whom?

## 2. Competitors and free substitutes (the lane is not empty)

| Player | What it does | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| [Mercor Enterprise Evals](https://www.mercor.com/enterprise-evals/) | Expert-built eval suites in under six weeks (Ramp: 160 finance tasks; Cognition: 200 coding tasks), priced per task, no public prices. Healthcare is not a named case. | About $2B gross run rate, over 30,000 weekly contractors, contractors paid 60-70% of revenue ([Dealroom](https://dealroom.co/news/137121-mercor-doubles-to-2b-gross-revenue-run-rate-as-ai-labs-buy-expert-data/)). The supply and sales motion exist; healthcare is one case study away. |
| [Vals AI](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks) | Proprietary **MedCode** (medical billing) and **MedScribe** (doctor admin work) benchmarks, plus finance, tax and legal. | $40M Series A at $400M valuation, revenue up 8x on 2025 ([Pulse 2.0](https://pulse2.com/vals-ai-raises-40-million-series-a-at-400-million-valuation-as-revenue-grows-8x/)). It already holds the "neutral referee" brand for back-office tasks. It tests models, not OASIS vendors. |
| [Centaur Labs](https://info.centaurlabs.com/complete-guide-to-medical-ai-data-labeling-in-2026) and [MDisrupt](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260108529541/en/) | Healthcare expert annotation and validation; Centaur claims 50,000+ experts, MDisrupt 4,000+ vetted. | Vertical expert benches already exist. No pricing found for either. |
| [AfterQuery](https://builtin.com/articles/afterquery-raises-30m-series-a-20260413) | Expert datasets and RL environments, about 100,000 experts. | $30M Series A at $300M. A reported $100M run rate appeared in one search summary but is not in the article I read, so treat it as unverified. |
| [Qualified Health](https://www.axios.com/pro/health-tech-deals/2026/03/25/ai-evaluation-startup-qualified-health-raises-125m-nea) | Health-system platform to evaluate, deploy and monitor AI. | $125M. Buyer-side assurance money goes to platforms. |
| [URAC AI accreditation](https://www.urac.org/blog/urac-health-care-ai-accreditation-launches-september-15) | Developer and user tracks, launched Sept 2025; first three accredited Aug 2026 ([URAC](https://www.urac.org/blog/guidehealth-rediminds-and-sandsrx-become-first-to-earn-urac-health-care-ai-accreditation/)). | It already occupies the "badge" slot. The announcement describes governance review, not accuracy testing, so an accuracy gap remains, but URAC can add one. |
| Home-health AI vendors' own QA | [Brellium](https://brellium.com/home-health) audits 100% of notes; [Enzo QA](https://www.homecaremag.com/news/enzo-health-funding-round-raises-20m-home-health-ai-solutions) reviews charts; Olli uses human coders to validate AI ([HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2025/01/first-choices-switch-to-olli-showcases-potential-for-ai-driven-cost-savings-in-home-health/)). | The "AI grading AI" layer is a product feature, not a service gap. |
| [Hippocratic AI](https://hippocraticai.com/real-world-evaluation-llm/) | Grades its agents in-house with 6,234 licensed clinicians. | The best-funded healthcare AI company builds this itself. |
| Free benchmarks and peer tests | HealthBench and MedHELM are free. On the advisor side, [XYPN's "Battle of the Bots"](https://www.xyplanningnetwork.com/advisor-blog/battle-of-the-bots-comparing-and-ranking-nine-ai-notetaker-solutions) hand-scored notetakers for accuracy (updated July 2026). | Advisors already get free peer accuracy tests from the network the father belongs to. |
| Vendor-written "comparisons" | e.g. [Copper Digital's OASIS AI mapping](https://www.copperdigital.com/blog/oasis-ai-mapping-which-platforms-automate-specific-oasis-items-in-2026). | Content marketing sets the free baseline for "a comparison". |

**Confirmed gap.** I found no independent or peer-reviewed accuracy study of AI-assisted OASIS tools. Vendor claims are self-reported, and nothing I found quantifies Brellium's accuracy either. The only reliability literature is on human OASIS coders ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4529994)).

## 3. Who pays, and what is the budget?

**Vendors (Enzo, Olli, Brellium, Apricot, Lime, Healthorbit, INMYTEAM, Roger and others).** They are funded: Enzo's $20M Series A was May 2026 ([HomeCare](https://www.homecaremag.com/news/enzo-health-funding-round-raises-20m-home-health-ai-solutions)), Apricot's came from [Insight Partners](https://www.insightpartners.com/ideas/apricot-announces-series-a-led-by-insight-partners-cementing-its-position-as-a-category-leader-in-post-acute-care/), and Brellium raised about $17M ([Axios](https://www.axios.com/pro/health-tech-deals/2025/04/17/brellium-raises-17m-healthcare-compliance-ai-automation)). But a vendor wants a badge, not an honest score. I found no source showing any home-health AI startup buying third-party accuracy tests. The nearest precedent failed: CHAI's assurance-lab network was scrapped partly because nobody settled who pays ([Fierce](https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/ai-and-machine-learning/inside-chais-failed-assurance-labs)). KLAS's vendor-funded model has drawn conflict-of-interest criticism; Allscripts dropped it for that reason ([HealthcareITToday](https://www.healthcareittoday.com/?p=15531)).

**Agencies (the better payer, but weakly evidenced).** Only 1.3% of 160 respondents were "very confident" in their agency's OASIS accuracy ([HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2025/06/how-ai-tools-help-home-health-providers-dramatically-lessen-oasis-time-burden/)). That was a vendor webinar poll about OASIS data collection, not about AI tools, so it shows a pain, not a purchase. CMS keeps coding responsibility with the assessing clinician, and software may not generate a final code ([Q1 2026 Q&A](https://qtso.cms.gov/system/files/qtso/CMS_OAI_Qtr_1_2026_QAs_April_2026_508c.pdf)). External reviewers are advisory only ([2024 Q&A](https://qtso.cms.gov/system/files/qtso/CMS_OAI_1st%20Qtr_2024_QAs_April_2024_final.pdf)). Agencies can plausibly afford it: MedPAC's March 2026 report reportedly shows fee-for-service margins of about 21% in 2024 ([MedPAC](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Mar26_Ch8_MedPAC_Report_To_Congress_SEC.pdf), figure from a search summary). The existing budget line is human OASIS and coding review at roughly $40-70 per chart ([HomeCare](https://www.homecaremag.com/may-2020/questions-outsourcing-partners), [Home Care Answers at $70](https://hcalive.azurewebsites.net/FAQ)). A pre-purchase bake-off competes for that line, and no one currently owns it.

**Advisor-tech vendors (weaker than home health).** Notetakers number over 15 and are consolidating ([InvestmentNews](https://www.investmentnews.com/advisor-tech/zeplyn-pivots-towards-agentic-ai-as-the-ai-notetaker-market-reaches-its-saturation-point/265655)). Platform-bundled tools are pushing prices toward $50 a seat ([InvestmentNews](https://www.investmentnews.com/advisor-tech/is-50-the-new-120-price-compression-comes-to-ai-notetakers/264773)). Jump and Zocks are funded ([Series Bs](https://www.investmentnews.com/advisor-tech/jump-and-zocks-raise-dueling-series-b-funding-rounds/265992)), but a squeezed category is a poor buyer of audits. The more interesting buyers are AI marketing-rule review startups: Blee raised $27M in September 2026 ([Axios](https://axios.com/pro/fintech-deals/2026/09/08/blee-27r-million-compliance-software)) and Archive Intel $6.3M ([Parsers](https://parsers.vc/news/251012-ai-drives-compliance-revolution--archive)). They compete with ACA and Smarsh. No source shows they buy outside evals.

**Reference prices.** Mercor's healthcare graders earn about $75-90 an hour for operations review and more for clinicians ([listing](https://work.mercor.com/jobs/list_AAABoGhoOEZyNZjl3PRFw4TN/clinical-health-care-operations-reviewer)). Mercor and Centaur publish no buyer prices. The only buyer-side price anchor I found is the CHAI-era estimate of "thousands of dollars" per assessment.

## 4. Reaching the first customers

- Vendors can be cold-emailed; there are perhaps 15-25 home-health AI vendors in total and a few dozen across advisor AI. The seed-stage founders are reachable but small buyers.
- Agencies gather at the National Alliance for Care at Home meeting, which ran [October 27-30, 2026](https://allianceforcareathome.org/event/2026-annual-meeting-expo/) and so is missed this year, and at Axxess's [AGILE](https://briefglance.com/articles/axxess-agile-2026-to-unveil-ai-leadership-blueprint-for-home-care) (May). Both are vendor-heavy. Finding the next dates is a to-do. State home-care associations and Home Health Care News readers are the warmer, cheaper channel.
- Large operators (Addus, Aveanna, Amedisys, Enhabit) show no public AI OASIS pilots in what I found. Addus described an internal AI committee focused on revenue cycle and scheduling. The enterprise signer for a bake-off is unknown.
- Health systems already evaluate third-party AI; 92% of surveyed organizations do, mostly in-house ([HCI](https://www.hcinnovationgroup.com/analytics-ai/ai-governance/news/55396163/survey-health-system-ai-validation-methods-vary-widely)). Agencies lack that capacity, which supports the buyer-side idea.

## 5. Legal, age and platform issues

- **Age and entity:** no wall. He is an adult and can form an LLC.
- **Benchmarking clauses.** Many AI vendors' terms bar publishing benchmark or performance results without consent ([examples](https://conductatlas.com/platform/luma-ai/luma-ai-terms-of-service/prohibition-on-publishing-benchmarks/); a monitoring site, not the contracts, so enforceability is unverified). A bake-off run under an agency's license, or a published index, could breach a vendor's terms. This is a real, underrated blocker for a "Ledger" that publishes scores.
- **Badge law.** A paid or affiliated "verified" seal is an endorsement with a material connection that must be disclosed, and it needs substantiation ([FKKS](https://advertisinglaw.fkks.com/post/102fhhn/when-using-a-third-party-seal-do-you-have-to-disclose-that-you-paid-to-use-it)). Vendor-funded scores invite the KLAS conflict critique. Publishing negative rankings of named vendors carries defamation and false-advertising risk that needs a lawyer.
- **HIPAA.** Synthetic charts built from nothing are low risk. Charts written from memory of real patients are not. Sources do not treat "synthetic" as automatically de-identified ([overview](https://www.accountablehq.com/post/hipaa-de-identification-requirements-safe-harbor-expert-determination-and-documentation)). Retainer evals on production traces would need BAAs.
- **Worker classification.** At fewer than 10 project-based experts it is minor. At scale it is the wall that Mercor, Handshake and Scale face: at least five suits in California and one in Texas ([Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/ai-data-trainers-suits-open-new-misclassification-fight-frontier)), plus a Scale settlement reported at $12.5M. Mercor also faced breach class actions after a March 2026 incident ([HR Dive](https://www.hrdive.com/news/ai-industry-recruiting-platform-faces-multiple-lawsuits-data-breach/817319/)).
- **Regulatory climate.** CMS froze new home-health agency enrollment for six months from May 13, 2026, citing fraud risk ([Federal Register](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-05-15/html/2026-09717.htm)). Ownership changes can count as new enrollments, which complicates sales of agencies. The SEC's 2026 exam priorities include the accuracy of firms' AI representations ([Foley](https://www.foley.com/insights/publications/2025/12/sec-releases-its-2026-examination-priorities/)).

## 6. Unit economics (mine, from sourced rates)

- A defensible 100-chart gold set takes about 2.25 expert hours per chart (write, second-code, adjudicate), or 225 hours. That figure comes from the gate and is unverified.
- At $32-38 an hour (a 2026-era per diem OASIS reviewer rate, [BerryDunn](https://careers-berrydunn.icims.com/jobs/3856/per-diem-coding-&-oasis-reviewer/job)) the build costs $7-9k. At $60-80 an hour (Mercor-level RN rates) it costs $13-18k.
- Even if pre-grading by AI cut expert hours by 60-70% (an assumption nobody has tested), the build is **$2-7k**. The $2,500 design-partner price is at or below break-even on the first set, and the $5,000 list price only just covers it.
- After the first set exists, a diagnostic is high-margin: marginal cost is running the vendor's output and adjudicating disagreements. But reusing a set contaminates a "blind" test, so a rotating hidden split is a recurring cost.
- A Mercor-rate bench is also a retention problem: his experts can earn more on Mercor directly, so the bench is not a moat.
- Realistic cost to first revenue is **$4-8k**, not the candidate's $1,500, and 8-12 weeks.

## 7. Size and the path to big

- **Vendor side.** Perhaps 40-80 targets across both verticals. At 15-25% buying $15-40k a year, revenue is **$0.1-0.8M a year** (mine). That is below the gate's $0.4-1.0M because advisor-AI is saturating.
- **Agency side.** A search summary citing MedPAC puts about 10,000 agencies treating traditional Medicare in 2024 (9,961; I did not read the primary table in [MedPAC's March 2026 chapter](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Mar26_Ch8_MedPAC_Report_To_Congress_SEC.pdf)). If 1-2% bought one $3-10k bake-off, that is **$0.3-2M**, one time, with no evidence of repeat spend. It also requires agencies to be mid-purchase on AI tools; Axxess's own survey says most organizations have not yet invested ([report](https://lifestyle.q923radio.com/story/9425/2026-industry-growth-insights-report-highlights-ai-opportunity-and-workforce-challenges-in-care-at-home/)).
- **Combined ceiling for the vertical:** roughly **$1-3M a year**, matching the gate. It is not $5-15M.
- **Big path 1: marketplace.** $50M of billings at a 35% take needs around 2,000 part-time experts and a weekly-pay float. Mercor already runs this with 30,000 experts and AfterQuery with 100,000. This is a venture fight he cannot win from a single vertical.
- **Big path 2: the standard.** "KLAS for AI accuracy" is the only coherent story. KLAS is estimated at about $42M of revenue ([FAQ](https://KLASresearch.com/faq); the revenue figure is the gate's estimate, unverified by me). But the slots are filling: URAC owns accreditation, Vals owns neutral benchmarks with a16z money, and Qualified Health owns health-system assurance. A standard also needs years of vendor trust and legal capital.
- **Round-1 failure modes, scored.** Small real market: yes. Hidden incumbents: yes (Vals MedCode, URAC, MDisrupt, Centaur). Wrong payer: yes for vendors, unproven for agencies. Price below cost: yes. Why-now partly used: yes, URAC and Mercor arrived first. Shrunk to survive: the sharpened "Ledger" is already that.

## 8. Why now (what is real)

- Home-health AI funding is hot (Enzo $20M, Brellium, Apricot, Olli) and OASIS-E2 and the April 2026 CMS Q&As make accuracy and clinician responsibility live questions.
- Health systems and regulators are asking vendors for proof ([HCI survey](https://www.hcinnovationgroup.com/analytics-ai/ai-governance/news/55396163/survey-health-system-ai-validation-methods-vary-widely)).
- But the same wave brought URAC (Sept 2025), Vals' $40M (Aug 2026) and Mercor's evals product, so the window for a first-mover standard is closing, not opening.

## 9. Verdict and the only test worth running

**Do not build the guild or a marketplace.** Rank F02 below ideas with a verified insider or a direct buyer. If the founder still wants it, run a three-week test before spending anything:

1. **Gate zero (this week):** resolve MHC (see section 1). If it sold to Choice or uses a vendor he would grade, drop the home-health "independent" framing.
2. **Buyer-first demand test:** pitch five agencies (family contacts first) a $3,000 buyer-side OASIS-vendor bake-off on 50 synthetic charts, with no vendor involvement and no badge. Success is **one agency paying before any vendor pays**. Zero takers in 21 days kills it.
3. **Price honestly:** at least $5,000 for any vendor diagnostic, with design-partner discounts only in exchange for written permission to publish anonymized results.
4. **Lawyer check, under $1k:** benchmark-clause exposure and publication risk, before any score leaves the building.

**What would move it to "strong":** an agency prepaying a bake-off, a vendor agreeing in writing to a published score, and a verified credentialed clinical lead who is not conflicted.

## Gaps

- MHC identity and the family's ownership: unresolved (the Florida corporate registry was blocked to me).
- No buyer prices for Mercor, Centaur or Vals evals.
- No evidence that any home-health AI startup has bought an outside accuracy test.
- The number of home-health AI vendors and the 2.25 hours per chart are estimates.
- The MedPAC agency count and the KLAS revenue are secondary or unverified.

# F03 CareFund: deep dossier (researched late Oct 2026)

**Verdict: WEAK, not dead. Do not build the product yet; run a 3-week demand test first.** The pain is real and the exact combination (home-care intake funnel + non-advice funding map + attorney/advisor fulfilment) is empty. But every piece is free, bundled by franchisors, or being sold top-down by funded companies. The one payer with a rational reason to pay per consult (elder-law attorneys) sits behind Florida Bar rules that force a multi-firm panel and therefore county density. My arithmetic puts the sponsorship-plus-license model's ceiling near $3-5M a year, well short of $10M+. Three gate claims are corrected below: the "why now" reimbursement squeeze, the advisor lead price, and how large Dad's firm appears in public records.

## 1. Who already does it (assume yes; they do)

**Funded, selling top-down (all active in 2026):**
- **CareScout (Genworth).** Nurse-led Care Plans went national in Jan 2026, local care advisors doubled in H1 to 26 states, first LTC policy approved in 35 states, Seniorly acquisition planned ([Business Wire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260120255657/en/), [Coverager](https://coverager.com/genworths-carescout-expands-nationwide-with-care-planning-and-provider-network/)). Gate: providers pay on placements. It owns the carrier channel the "big" path needs.
- **Carefull.** $16.5M Series A, $19.7M total, plus CIBC debt in June 2025 ([VentureBeat](https://venturebeat.com/business/cibc-innovation-banking-provides-growth-financing-to-carefull-to-accelerate-expansion)). Sold to credit unions through [CUNA Strategic Services](https://www.cunastrategicservices.com/content/cuna/css/become-a-provider/all-providers/Carefull/carefull-for-wealth-advisors.html). In June 2026 Edward Jones invested and offered it free to all US clients across 20,000+ advisors ([FinTech Global](https://fintech.global/2026/06/25/edward-jones-backs-carefull-with-venture-investment/)). Cetera advisors have had it since Jan 2023 ([Rethinking65](https://rethinking65.com/cetera-advisors-have-access-to-platform-helping-older-clients)).
- **Cariloop.** $20M Series C (2024); firm-level wealth deals with Raymond James (Dec 2025), Quotient Wealth (Apr 1, 2026) and Mariner (Jul 2026, $647B in assets) ([Cariloop](https://cariloop.com/news/cariloop-quotient-partnership), [InvestmentNews](https://www.investmentnews.com/retirement-planning/mariner-adds-caregiving-support-as-advisors-flag-rising-client-need/267293)). Wealth firms are buying caregiver support as an enterprise benefit, which closes the door on "individual advisor pays per consult" for any advisor at those firms.
- **Tendercare.** A free family platform with a vetted "Trusted Network" including a financial-advisor track; "membership is never sold; it's earned" ([advisor page](https://trytendercare.com/financial-advisors)). In Apr 2026 it named Assisting Hands (134 offices) a national homecare partner ([Home Care](https://www.homecaremag.com/news/tendercare-partners-assisting-hands-home-care-vivo-fitness)). Its monetization is not disclosed. This is the closest shape to CareFund and it already has a franchise-distribution deal.
- **Baba** (Feb 2026, $6.5M seed from General Catalyst, human-plus-AI advocacy for older adults) is adjacent; the only source is a weak aggregator ([BriefGlance](https://briefglance.com/articles/baba-exits-stealth-with-65m-to-transform-elder-care-with-ai-and-humans)).

**Free or bundled substitutes (these cap what anyone pays):**
- **Franchise agencies give the claim help away.** Amada brands itself "America's trusted resource for caregiving and long-term care insurance claims advocacy," offers free LTCI claims processing, and runs a preferred-partner network of agents, advisors, carriers and elder-law attorneys that swap referrals ([Amada](https://www.amadaseniorcare.com/partner/)). Home Helpers and CareWorks also offer free claim help ([Home Helpers](https://www.homehelpershomecare.com/bradenton/resources/long-term-care-insurance-assistance/), [CareWorks](https://www.careworkshealthservices.com/long-term-care-insurance/free-ltci-claims-processing/)).
- **The agency-to-attorney referral already flows for free.** A networking site ranks home health care the #1 referral source for elder-law attorneys and financial advisors #3 ([PTBN](https://ptbn.us/where-to-network/attorney-elder-law/); low-quality source, directional only).
- **NCOA BenefitsCheckUp** screens for 2,500+ programs; nearly 9.9M people found $42.7B since 2001 ([Federal Register 2022](https://govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2022-05-11/pdf/2022-10094.pdf)). The generic funding map is a commodity.
- **CMS GUIDE** funds dementia care navigation for 8 years from July 2024 with up to $2,500 a year of respite per patient and 292 participants ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/priorities/innovation/innovation-models/guide)).

**Pay-per-lead price anchors:** SmartAsset charges advisors per lead with a monthly budget and no upfront fee ([SmartAsset](https://getleads.smartasset.com/smartadvisor-referral-sign-up/)). Third-party figures are $90-190 per lead (RIABiz 2018, repeated in [Kitces 2021](https://www.kitces.com/blog/the-latest-in-financial-advisortech-july-2021/)) and $100-200 per lead or $2-3k per acquired client ([WealthManagement](https://www.wealthmanagement.com/growth-strategies/top-qualified-lead-sources-for-advisors)). The idea's "$150-300+" is the high end. ElderLawAnswers lists an attorney for **$175 a month** ($2,100 a year), with no lead guarantee ([pricing](https://join.elderlawanswers.com/pricing/)); NAELA dues were listed at about $595 a year (possibly outdated). Caring.com bills home-care partners per lead or per start of care but publishes no price ([Caring.com](https://partners.caring.com/get-leads-caring-com)).

## 2. Payers, budgets and unit economics

**Agencies (the distribution, a weak payer).** Home-care marketing averages about 1.1% of revenue ([Home Care Pulse via HomeCareAtlas](https://homecareatlas.com/blog/home-care-marketing-spend-gap)); home health and long-term care average 1-2% ([Forvis Mazars via NDPAP](https://ndpap.org/resources/for-providers/digital-marketing-benchmarks-for-independent-hospice-and-home-health-agencies)). On HomeCareAtlas's illustrative $100K-a-month agency that is about $1,100 a month in total marketing, so the gate's **$300-900 a month license is 27-82% of the whole budget.** Typical lead cost is $80-150 and one admission $150-400, but those are vendor estimates (single-source Sagapixel; NDPAP labels its channel figures estimates).

The agency's real prize is large: the 2025 Florida median for non-medical caregiving is **$73,216 a year (about $6,100 a month, up 7%)**, with a national median of $35 an hour ([CareScout Florida release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260302523108/en/CareScout-Releases-2025-Cost-of-Care-Data-for-Florida); the monthly figure is my division). One retained or converted private-pay family is worth tens of thousands. So an outcome-priced pilot (pay if conversion rises) is more credible than a flat license. I found **no price comparable for "conversion and retention help"**; every comparable buys new leads, not existing census.

**Elder-law attorneys (the rational per-consult payer).** Secondary sources put Medicaid-planning engagements at $3-15k ([ThePricer](https://www.thepricer.org/how-much-does-a-medicaid-lawyer-cost/); an attorney-authored page guesses about $10k, [ElderLawAnswers](https://attorney.elderlawanswers.com/how-much-will-medicaid-planning-and-application-cost-12408)). A common law-firm rule is acquisition cost at about 10% of client value, and vendors cite $75 geo-targeted leads and $1-3k workshops converting 20-40% of attendees ([Marketing Lawcast](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1806835/episodes/15970318-learn-how-to-create-more-effective-ads-that-fit-your-budget); vendor claims). At a $5k fee and 30% close, 10% CAC is roughly **$150 per qualified consult, $300 at $10k.** That is the ceiling, below the idea's $200-350.

**Flat-fee advisors (Dad's roster, the wrong payer).** A 45-minute consult at hourly rates around $257-270 (2020 study) earns about $190-270 ([Wealth Briefing](https://www.wealthbriefing.com/html/article.php?id=189525); flat plans averaged $2,926 in 2026, [ThinkAdvisor](https://www.thinkadvisor.com/amp/2026/05/04/average-financial-planning-retainer-fee-surges-52-in-3-years)). A $200-350 lead fee is 100%+ of revenue. Confirmed dead as a revenue engine.

**Funnel math (my model; the 10% and 15% rates are the gate's untested guesses).** 200 admissions x 10% complete the intake x 15% book = **about 3 consults per agency per year**, roughly $750 of lead value at $250. Agency license revenue, not leads, would have to carry the business, and the agency budget cannot. For a 4-attorney county panel to pay $300 a month each ($14.4k a year) at about $200 per consult, you need about 72 consults, so **about 25 participating agencies in one county.** Only Miami-Dade, Broward, Palm Beach, Hillsborough, Orange and Pinellas are plausible. That is the chicken-and-egg: agencies must be nearly free to reach density, but then attorneys fund everything, which raises the patient-brokering question below.

**Size.** Agency counts are murky: HomeCareAtlas lists 15,565 and estimates 53,950 ([HomeCareAtlas](https://homecareatlas.com/guide/agencies-by-state)); about 12,000 are Medicare-certified (secondary). The Florida Bar Elder Law Section has about 1,800 members (undated, [Florida Bar](https://www.floridabar.org/the-florida-bar-news/bars-elder-law-section-serves-an-often-vulnerable-clientele/)); NAELA has 4,200+. My arithmetic: 500 agencies x $3.6k + 10% of 4,200 attorneys x $3.6k is about **$3.3M**. This matches the gate's $0.7M year-5 median at lower adoption. Reaching $10M+ needs a payer class nobody has shown. The LTCI hook is narrow: about 6.9M people are covered and $16.9B was paid in 2024 ([AHIP](https://ahiporg-production.s3.amazonaws.com/documents/202511-AHIP_LTCStateData.pdf)), and carriers already have CareScout and Carefull.

## 3. Where the first customers are

- **Family agency (MHC).** Free 60-day pilot at the admission and discharge desks is the only no-search channel. It produces a favor-sale, not proof.
- **Agencies:** the Home Care Association of Florida (HCAF). HomeCareCon 2026 was the 37th edition in Orlando with 600+ professionals ([Simitree](https://simitreehc.com/events/homecarecon-37th-annual-conference-and-trade-show)); I found **no 2027 date**. HCAF runs monthly webinars (a Dec 15, 2026 Medicare-certified session) and the Home Care Association of America has a Florida chapter ([HCAOA](https://www.hcaoa.org/newsletters/category/florida)). Franchise owners (Amada, Home Helpers, Visiting Angels) already publish "how to pay" content and are the warmest peers.
- **Attorneys:** the Elder Law Section and AFELA, NAELA's Florida chapter. The Section's annual update has historically been in January ([2023 event page](https://www.floridabar.org/event/elder-law-annual-update/)); confirm 2027.
- **Advisors:** FPA, NAPFA and XYPN chapters, not Dad's roster. Cold outreach by an 18-year-old to attorneys or agency owners will be weak; plan on warm introductions only.

## 4. Legal and platform issues (none is a wall; each needs counsel)

1. **Fla. Stat. 817.505 (patient brokering).** It applies to "any person"; penalties run from a third-degree felony and $50k to a first-degree felony and $500k at 20+ patients. There is **no general exemption for flat advertising fees**. The closest fit is (3)(i), payments to an information service that provides free consumer information, does not steer to particular providers, offers no counseling, and charges advance, fair-market fees not based on patient value ([statute](https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2024/817.505)). Design: CareFund is the payee; sponsorships flat; panel rotating; no per-start fees; nothing flows to the agency.
2. **Florida Bar Rule 4-7.22.** CareFund is a "qualifying provider": 4+ firms on the panel, no fee-sharing or percentage fees, annual lawyer list to the Bar ([rule text](https://floridajustice.com/rule/4-7-22/), [Bar guidance](https://www.floridabar.org/ethics/etad/qualifying-providers-lawyer-referral-services/)). A 2018 Board proposal would bar lawyers from taking referrals from entities that also receive a benefit for referring to nonlegal professionals ([Bar News](https://www.floridabar.org/the-florida-bar-news/amendment-would-prohibit-referrals-from-entities-that-also-steer-clients-to-nonlegal-professionals/)). **I could not confirm adoption.** If in force, one platform sending families to both lawyers and advisors is a problem.
3. **Unlicensed practice of law.** The Florida Supreme Court held that nonlawyers drafting Medicaid-planning documents (QITs, personal-service contracts) or advising how to apply Florida law to obtain Medicaid is UPL; preparing the application itself is allowed ([Bar News](https://www.floridabar.org/the-florida-bar-news/court-oks-medicaid-planning-upl-opinion/), [Justia](https://law.justia.com/cases/florida/supreme-court/2015/sc14-211.html)). **The part families most want, spend-down strategy, is exactly the line CareFund cannot cross**, so the funding map stays generic and overlaps the free NCOA tool.
4. **SEC Marketing Rule.** Paid referral from advisors makes CareFund a promoter: written agreement, client disclosure, no written-agreement exemption once compensation exceeds $1,000 in 12 months ([Kitces](https://www.kitces.com/blog/sec-marketing-rule-advisers-promoters-solicitors-testimonial-endorsement-referrals/)). Workable (SmartAsset does it) but I found no evidence advisors will pay for a promoter-compliance rail.
5. **HIPAA marketing.** A communication encouraging a third party's product is marketing unless it fits the treatment and care-coordination exceptions, which do not cover lawyers or advisors; "financial remuneration" is direct or indirect payment from the third party whose product is described ([45 CFR 164.501](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/part-164/section-164.501)). My reading: the trigger is money flowing from attorneys or advisors to the agency. A sponsor-subsidized "free" tool may count as indirect; get a healthcare lawyer's view.
6. **VA.** Unaccredited parties cannot charge for VA claim help; the federal GUARD VA Benefits Act has not passed (H.R. 1732, [tracker](https://www.thelobbynews.com/congress/bills/119/house-bill/1732)). Keep VA content informational.

## 5. Why now: what holds up, what does not

- **CMS moratorium: holds, with a clock.** No new Medicare home-health agencies or branches since May 13, 2026, six months (expires Nov 13 unless extended); CMS promised about 60 days' notice and I found none ([HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2026/10/the-future-for-hospice-home-health-providers-under-cms-moratoria/), [Mintz](https://www.mintz.com/insights-center/viewpoints/2146/2026-05-18-cms-imposes-nationwide-enrollment-freeze-home-health)). It is Medicare-only and blocks de novos and sales; I found no evidence it changes agency spending on private-pay conversion.
- **Reimbursement squeeze: overstated.** The gate cited a cut. The CY2027 proposed rule is a net **+2.4% ($420M)**: a 2.1% update, no new permanent adjustment for the first time since CY2022, and a one-year -3.0% temporary adjustment ([CMS fact sheet](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/calendar-year-cy-2027-home-health-prospective-payment-system-proposed-rule-fact-sheet-cms-1844-p)). MedPAC urged -7%, so the final rule (due about now) could still change.
- **Demand: holds.** 63M caregivers (AARP, via the Mariner article), and only 43% of caregivers have sought professional financial guidance (Edward Jones/Age Wave, same article). That supports need but not who pays.
- **Capital arriving in 2026 is both validation and crowding.** Edward Jones/Carefull, Cariloop/Mariner, Tendercare/Assisting Hands and CareScout/Seniorly all landed this year.

## 6. Unverified and load-bearing

- **MHC Healthcare.** Search found no Florida home-health company by that name; matches were an Arizona health-center network, a Maryland clinic group and Medical House Calls, none confirmed as the family company. Type (Medicare-certified, private duty, both) decides the pilot. Check AHCA's Florida Health Finder, Care Compare and Sunbiz, or ask directly.
- **MyFinancialAdvice.** An auto-generated profile shows MYFINANCIALADVICE, INC. in Boulder as an SEC-registered adviser with about 2 employees ([Advisoros](https://www.theadvisoros.com/advisors/colorado/boulder/richard-byhre-1047)); I found nothing on Ron Peremel or an advisor network. The "pre-screened flat-fee roster" must be confirmed before it is a customer source.
- **Agency intake and booking rates** (10% and 15%) and any lift in private-pay conversion or length of stay are untested; this is the one number peers would pay for.
- **Whether a Bar-compliant panel can be filled** with 4 firms per county who each pay.

## 7. Scorecard against the six tests

1. **First paid customer in 60-90 days, under $10k: 6/10.** Likely via family pilot and a few advisors at $99, but counsel pushes cost to about $6-10k and revenue is favors.
2. **Reachable peers within 6 months: 5/10.** Warm intros to 2-3 agencies; no event in the window; no conversion proof.
3. **No license wall: 5/10.** None needed, but four regimes (patient brokering, Bar 4-7.22, UPL, SEC promoter) stack, plus HIPAA.
4. **Uses real edges: 7/10.** AI-speed build, rules database, family agency access. Gen Z distribution is not an edge here.
5. **Path to big: 2/10.** About $0.7M median and $3-5M by my math; $10M+ needs channels held by CareScout, Carefull and Cariloop.
6. **Not crowded: 3/10.** The combination is empty; every component is funded, free or franchisor-bundled.

## 8. Recommendation and kill test

Do not write software. Spend 3 weeks and under $1,000 on a paper test:

1. **Week 1:** verify MHC's licenses and ask Dad what MFA's advisors actually do. Interview 12 agency owners on one question: how many families a year leave or cut hours because of cost, and what they pay for conversion today.
2. **Weeks 2-3:** co-host one "Paying for Care" session at the family agency with one elder-law attorney, using a printed funding checklist and no software. Count families who book a consult.
3. **Kill if** by week 6 fewer than 2 attorneys will sign a written intent to pay at least $250 per qualified consult or $300 a month, **or** fewer than 3 of 12 agency owners rank conversion or retention in their top three problems. The gate's April 2027 test (3 of 10 agencies at $300 a month) is the second gate, after a build.

If it passes, sell the **attorney-sponsored, agency-distributed workshop and consult funnel in dense Florida counties** as a regional service. Treat anything bigger as unproven.

## 1. Bottom line

**Verdict: weak, about 3/10. Run the free two-week premise test, but do not commit to this as the company.**

- **The audit leg is real but small, and the market is now crowded from two directions.** Five funded horizontal vendors do remit-versus-contract repricing. Three funded *post-acute-first* vendors the gate missed (Claim Health, Enzo Health, Advanced RevCycle) already sit inside home-health billing workflows and can add underpayment detection.
- **The benchmark leg is the only venture-scale piece, and it has the worst legal and demand uncertainty.** "See how your MA rates rank against peers" is exactly the feature antitrust commentary warns about. No evidence that owners will pay for it.
- **The insider premise is unresolved, and it now has two competing readings** (section 2). If "MHC Healthcare" is not a home-health agency group, the pilot leg collapses.
- **It is cheap to test.** One conversation with his mother, one BAA, and 3 months of remits tell him whether the audit leg has any money in it.

## 2. The insider premise: what is "MHC Healthcare"?

Two public entities fit the name. Neither is verified as his grandfather's company.

1. **Florida home-health reading (the gate's).** NPPES lists seven Florida home-health entities named "MHC Area N, LLC". One record shows MHC Area 9, LLC (Boca Raton) doing business as Choice Health at Home and Haven Home Health Care, with Katrina Lanier as secretary and authorized official, in-network for Florida Blue and UnitedHealthcare marketplace plans ([NPI profile, third-party aggregator](https://npiprofile.com/npi/1245899020)). An authorized official is a filing role, not proof of ownership.
2. **Maryland injury-clinic reading (new).** MHC HealthCare, legal name Maryland Healthcare Clinics LLC, has operated since 1987, was founded by Dr. Semyon Friedman, and lists more than 130 clinics (physical therapy, orthopedics, neurology, physiatry, radiology) in Delaware, Florida, Maryland, North Carolina, Virginia and D.C., with a personal-injury focus and an attorney records portal ([MHC About](https://mhcorp.com/about), [MHC home](https://mhcorp.com)). Its pages do not mention Medicare or Medicare Advantage. A separate Arizona "MHC Healthcare" is a community health center network, not a match ([Marana Health redirect](https://maranahealth.org/?p=728)).

**Why it matters.** The MA remit thesis only works if the first customer is a Medicare-certified home-health or SNF operator. A personal-injury and PT clinic chain bills auto, attorney-letter and commercial payers. Repricing against fee schedules might still work there, but the "peer owners" would be injury clinics, a segment under active insurer fraud litigation in Florida in 2026 (for example [GEICO's August 2026 suit against Miami PIP clinics](https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/us/news/risk-compliance-legal/geico-says-three-miami-clinics-billed-1-35-million-in-false-nofault-claims-586535.aspx); I found no allegation involving MHC). Data sharing and benchmarks would be a harder sell there.

**Action:** Ask his mother for the legal entity name, the NPIs, and what share of revenue is Medicare Advantage. Everything below assumes the home-health reading.

## 3. Is the problem real?

**Evidence for rate and payment leakage (mostly qualitative):**
- MA home-health payment is usually **per visit by discipline**, with some case rates and a few PDGM-like episodic deals. Contract terms vary on timely filing, clean-claim definitions and payment timelines, and underpayments "need auditing against contracted rates" ([Enzo Health glossary](https://www.enzo.health/glossary/medicare-advantage-home-health)). So repricing is deterministic and close to a freight tariff problem. Note it is per-visit math, not "percent of PDGM".
- Elara Caring's executive said a good MA partner has "good contract loads" and is willing to fix contract-load errors ([Home Health Care News, 2024](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2024/06/how-home-health-providers-get-what-they-want-out-of-ma-plans/)). That names the mechanism: plans load rates wrong.
- One hospital-based chain found negative margins on about 90% of its managed-care contracts, and settled with an MA plan for about $1.2M over three years using 42 CFR 422.214 ([AAPC case study](https://aapc.com/codes/coding-newsletters/my-homecare-week-alert/case-study-heres-how-one-hha-used-regs-to-recover-managed-care-payments-113604-article); undated, likely years old, and that case was a non-contract rate dispute, not a contract-load error).
- Agencies subsidize MA rates according to NAHC's 2014 and 2020 surveys; a 2024 NAHC/HHFMA MA survey ran, but I found no published results ([NAHC community post](https://community.allianceforcareathome.org/discussion/nahchhfma-medicare-advantage-survey-your-input-matters-3)).

**Evidence against (or missing):**
- I found **no published case of MA plans mis-paying home health against contract at scale**. Hospital underpayment is cited at 0.5-1% (R1) to 1-3% (HFMA, via vendor) of net patient revenue, and both are vendor-reported and not home-health specific ([MD Clarity comparison](https://www.mdclarity.com/comparison/best-healthcare-underpayment-recovery-services)).
- The documented MA pain in home health is rates below fee-for-service, authorizations and denials, not rate-load errors. Frontpoint's CEO: many large providers "assume a good rate is parity with Medicare, and that's not a reality" ([HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2024/06/how-home-health-providers-get-what-they-want-out-of-ma-plans/)). A benchmark helps *negotiation*; an audit only helps if there is leakage.
- A contracted provider generally cannot use the MA payment-dispute channel (that is for non-contracted providers), so recovery runs through the contract's own dispute clause, with windows the gate put at roughly 60-125 days ([UHC non-contracted dispute rights](https://preview-gateway.uhcprovider.com/content/dam/provider/docs/public/health-plans/medicare/MA-Non-Cont-Provider-Dispute-Appeal-Rights.pdf); gate for the window range, which I did not independently verify). A 12-month retro sweep is partly time-barred, so the durable product is continuous monitoring.
- MedPAC finds MA enrollees use home health slightly less than fee-for-service (8.3% vs 8.6%) ([MedPAC June 2025, Ch. 3](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Jun25_Ch3_MedPAC_Report_To_Congress_SEC.pdf)), and hospice is out of scope because it is paid by Original Medicare after the carve-in demonstration ended in 2024 ([CMS VBID](https://www.cms.gov/priorities/innovation/innovation-models/VBID)).

## 6. First customers and how to reach them

- **Customer 1: MHC**, if the Florida home-health reading holds. Multiple LLCs means multiple contract sets. Caveat: a related-party pilot proves the mechanics but gives weak third-party proof; peers will discount "verified by their billing lead".

That is a ready-made hook: offer to analyze the member data. I found no 2027 convention date. Healthcare CPAs and billers (white-label) are the other lane; the Florida Health Care Association (SNFs) holds its 2027 conference July 25-29 in Orlando ([listing](https://reliant-rehab.com/events/florida-health-care-association-annual-conference-trade-show/)).
- **Credibility wall:** an agency CFO sending remits to an 18-year-old needs family sponsorship plus agency-side de-identification. Cold outreach should be expected to fail.

## 7. Legal, age and platform issues

- **Age:** not a barrier to forming an LLC, signing a BAA, or taking payment. HIPAA business-associate duties apply regardless. The Security Rule overhaul is not final; final action is now projected for July 2027, so the current rule governs and risk-analysis failures are OCR's top enforcement target ([McDermott](https://www.mcdermottlaw.com/insights/final-action-on-hipaa-security-rule-modifications-now-projected-for-july-2027/)).
- **Percentage fees:** the OIG's 1998 third-party billing guidance flags percentage compensation as an upcoding risk, the Medicare reassignment rule bars agent pay tied to dollars billed or collected where the agent receives the payment, and commentary says Florida bars percentage fees for Medicaid ([AAPC/Foley summary](https://www.aapc.com/codes/coding-newsletters/my-medicare-compliance-reimbursement-alert/compliance-flat-fee-billing-contracts-could-reduce-risk-120670-article)). Pure variance analysis where the provider keeps receiving the payments is lower risk, but a health lawyer must sign off. **Fallback: flat diagnostic plus a fixed fee per resolved dispute**, which also differentiates from pure contingency.
- **Antitrust (benchmark leg):** DOJ withdrew its health-care information-exchange safety zones in February 2023 and the FTC in July 2023 ([Hogan Lovells](https://www.hoganlovells.com/en/publications/ftc-joins-doj-in-rescinding-health-care-antitrust-policies)). DOJ and FTC opened a public inquiry on replacement guidance on Feb 23, 2026 ([Arnold & Porter](https://arnoldporter.com/en/perspectives/publications/2026/04/antitrust-agency-insights-developments-at-the-us-antitrust-enforcement-agencies-first-quarter-2026)). After the May 2026 Agri Stats settlement, counsel-commentary lists risk reducers as a data lag of at least 45 days, three or more contributors per cell, a cap on any one contributor's share, and re-identification checks, and flags participant lists, rankings and contributor-count flags as disfavored ([Frier Levitt](https://www.frierlevitt.com/articles/agri-stats-settlement-healthcare-information-exchanges-antitrust/); that is a law firm's extrapolation to health care). **The pitch "see how you rank against peers" must become "your realized yield versus an anonymized band".**
- **MA contract confidentiality:** the design (owners enter percent-of-Medicare figures they control, never documents) is plausible but untested; counsel must confirm. Gate estimate: $10-25k.
- **Florida prompt-pay law** (12% simple interest on overdue claims, [s. 641.3155](https://m.flsenate.gov/Statutes/641.3155)) might give leverage, but whether it applies to MA plans, given federal preemption, is a question for counsel.
- **He must not code, bill or submit claims.** No license is needed for variance analysis.

| Mid | $2.5M | 1.0% | $25k | $5.6k |
| High | $4.0M | 2.0% | $80k | $18k |

- **Audit-only Florida ceiling:** 100-250 reachable agencies at the mid case is $0.6-1.4M if he won all of them. At a realistic 15% share it is about $85-210k a year. That is a side business.
- **National:** 12,409 certified agencies, perhaps 1,500-3,000 large enough (gate). At a $12k blended price that is $18-36M at 100% share. Reaching $10M ARR needs about 700-800 customers: roughly 25% of the big-agency pool, which is the "heroic share" case the lessons file says to call dead.
- **Second vertical improves it but is unproven:** about 14,700 SNFs ([MedPAC via search](https://medpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Mar25_Ch6_MedPAC_Report_To_Congress_SEC.pdf)), where per-diem MA contracts are simpler to reprice and MA discharge share is high (47.6% of MA enrollee hospital discharges went to SNF in 2024 per [Becker's/Plante Moran](https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/post-acute/medicare-advantage-snf-utilization-grows-6-more-notes-plante-moran-report/)). At $15k, 670 SNFs is $10M (about 4.5% share). That requires a separate build and a different champion.
- **Cost to first revenue:** about $6k per the gate (lawyer review $1.5-3k, HIPAA risk analysis plus cyber/E&O $2-4k; the gate's estimates). Timeline reality: a flat diagnostic could pay in 8-11 weeks if MHC agrees; contingency cash lags because plans take weeks to respond, so first recovered dollars probably land in month 5-7.

## 9. Why now

- Florida loses more MA plans for 2027 than any state, 611 down to 560 ([Florida Trend](https://www.floridatrend.com/news/2026/10/20/florida-trend-health-care/)), driven by Humana and UnitedHealthcare exits; Dec. 7 is the enrollment deadline. Re-contracting pressure is real in Q4 2026-Q1 2027.
- CY2027 home-health proposed rule: +2.4% aggregate ($420M), but it keeps a -3.0% temporary adjustment ([Trella](https://www.trellahealth.com/resource-center/blog/six-months-in-what-the-cy2026-home-health-final-rule-is-telling-the-market-and-what-to-watch-for-in-2027/)). Margin pressure persists, so owners hunt for MA dollars.
- CMS froze new Medicare enrollment of home-health agencies and hospices nationwide for six months from May 13, 2026, ending around mid-November unless extended (my arithmetic) ([Venable](https://www.venable.com/insights/publications/2026/05/cms-announces-nationwide-six-month-medicare)). This protects incumbents and raises the value of existing agencies, but it also signals a fraud-scrutiny climate.
- The funding wave (Tenix, Anomaly, Claim Health, Enzo) validates the category and shrinks his window. **Why-now is also why-crowded.**

## 10. Scoring against the six criteria

| Criterion | Score | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| 1. First paying customer in 60-90 days, under $10k | 5/10 | Flat diagnostic possible by week 8-11 if MHC is a home-health group; contingency cash is later; related-party revenue |
| 2. Reachable buyers | 5/10 | HCAF, owners, CPAs are reachable; credibility and data-handover wall is real |
| 3. No license wall | 6/10 | No license; HIPAA, fee-structure and (later) antitrust counsel needed |
| 4. Uses his edges | 5/10 | Freight-audit engine reuse is real; contract ingestion is the hard part and is commoditized by LLMs; true edge is family access, not tech |
| 5. Path to $10M+ | 2/10 | Audit is boutique; benchmark is unproven and legally exposed; SNF is a second build |
| 6. Not crowded | 2/10 | Five horizontal and three post-acute-first funded players |

**Overall about 3/10** (gate median-case $1.5M and upside case $15M a year are consistent with this).

## 11. Recommendation and kill tests

1. **Day 1:** Resolve the MHC question with his mother (entity, NPIs, MA share). If it is the injury-clinic chain, drop this idea for that pilot and re-score.
2. **Weeks 1-2:** Get 3 months of de-identified 835s and the top three plan rate exhibits under a BAA. **Kill the contingency leg if variance is under 1% of MA paid**; take it seriously only at 1.5% or more.
3. **In parallel:** Offer HCAF a free analysis of their MA member survey, in exchange for introductions. **Kill the benchmark leg if fewer than three non-family owners agree to contribute data.**
4. **Do not spend legal money** (fee review, antitrust design) until step 2 shows real variance.
5. **Price first deals as flat diagnostic plus a fixed fee per resolved dispute**, not a bare percentage.

## Gaps

- No source for MA's share of agency revenue or episodes in Florida for 2025-2026; no published MA home-health underpayment-at-scale study; NAHC/HHFMA 2024 results not public.
- I could not fetch the HCAF "Medicare Advantage under the microscope" article (403) or Claim Health's press release (403), so their exact product scope (underpayment detection yes or no) is unconfirmed.
- Tenix's round rests on one trade-wire source; the $12k SHP price is from an AI-assisted aggregator.
- Dispute-window range (60-125 days), Florida concentration data, and the $2-4k compliance costs come from the gate and are not independently re-verified.
- The MHC identity is unconfirmed on both readings.

# F04 Dossier: Day-90 Aide Network (pay-on-retention aide recruiting, Florida)

Researched 2 Nov 2026. Evidence quality is flagged inline. "Inference" means my own reasoning, not a sourced fact.

## 1. Verdict

**Stays WEAK. Fast to first dollar, but it fails the "big" test and the "not crowded" test as written.**

- The exact pricing (pay at start plus day 90) is unoccupied, but I found no seller of it. That is a pricing wrapper, not a moat. Every vendor below could add it in a quarter (inference).
- The tri-county pool is about $19M a year at $900 per retained aide (section 7). A $10M business needs about 13,000 retained hires a year across five or six metros. That is an operations-heavy staffing business, not software.
- The first dollar is real. A family pilot could pay in roughly 8 weeks, and I found no license wall for W-2 recruiting (section 5).
- The fix is not a bigger fee. It is to sell the retention service first, because retention is the variable the fee depends on and the one nobody sells to non-medical agencies in Creole and Spanish (section 9).

## 2. Who already does this

| Player | Model and price | Threat |
|---|---|---|
| [CareRecruit](https://carerecruit.io/) | Meta and Google ads plus AI screening. Flat monthly retainer per location, one agency per market, no guarantee, no price shown. A Florida owner testimonial. Languages not mentioned. | Medium |
| [Carework](https://www.careworkus.com/learnmore) | AI voice recruiter from $720/mo. Done-for-you from $1,865/mo. Claims 35,000+ caregivers hired. No guarantee. | High on price |
| [Care Hero](https://www.gocarehero.com/) | AI phone screening, subscription, 30-day money-back pilot. Customers include Home Instead, BrightStar, Amada and HomeWell. | Medium |
| [Boostpoint](https://boostpoint.com/industries-healthcare/home-health-aide-recruiting/) | Meta job ads, $750/mo minimum ad budget. Own benchmark: $3.76 median cost per applicant, 31% apply rate. It publishes no cost per hire. | High (cheapest sourcing) |
| [Carefam](https://techfundingnews.com/14-5m-for-carefam-ai-agents-to-fix-healthcare-hiring-bottleneck/) | A $14.5M-funded AI hiring layer covering recruiting, scheduling, credential checks and onboarding for acute, long-term and home care. Pricing and languages undisclosed. | Rising |
| [EngineHire](https://enginehire.io/caregiver-retention-and-turnover-for-home-care-2026/) | Software with automated welcome sequences, first-shift reminders and scheduled check-ins. Pricing hidden. | Overlaps the concierge |
| [Home Care Marketing](https://www.homecaremarketing.com/pricing/) | Marketing bundles at $997 to $2,999/mo, with a caregiver pipeline and career site. | Low |
| [Truffle](https://www.hiretruffle.com/blog/where-to-find-home-health-aides) | AI video screening, plans from $49/mo. | Low |
| [Well Beyond Care](https://markets.financialcontent.com/concordmonitor/article/einpresswire-2021-6-30-well-beyond-care-offers-caregiver-recruitment-service-to-organizations) | A 2021 launch with a small fee per caregiver connected. I could not find evidence it grew. | Precedent only |
| Staffing agencies | [Mark up aide wages 45 to 60%](https://boostpoint.com/industries-healthcare/caregiver-staffing-agency-cost/) (a vendor figure). | Different product |

**Free or captive substitutes**

- CareerSource boards give employers free recruitment help. Broward's flyer offers [on-the-job-training reimbursement of up to 75% of wages, free job posting and virtual job fairs](https://careersourcebroward.com/assets/uploads/documents/CSBD-Flyers-for-Webpage/Employer-Summary-Of-Services-PDF_rev1.pdf). The flyer is dated 2020. CareerSource South Florida's page says [up to 50%](https://www.careersourcesfl.com/training-incentives). I could not confirm that home health aide roles qualify.
- The employer-owned pipeline is already built. United HomeCare and Sunshine Health run [free 40-hour aide training with immediate placement at United HomeCare](https://www.sunshinehealth.com/newsroom/sunshine-health-and-united-homecare-join-forces-to-addres-home-health-labor-shortage-in-south-florida.html). [Florida Memorial University partners with United HomeCare](https://www.fmu.edu/?p=7620) on the same pathway. Large non-profits do not need a middleman. Schools such as [FVI](https://fvi.edu/home-health-aides/home-health-aide-training) are the independent supply.
- Employee referral bonuses are the default substitute. Miami postings show [HomeWell paying up to $300 after 90 days](https://career.com/job/homewell-care-services/caregiver-hha-cna-english-speaker/j202501212256486565642) and [ComForCare $250 after 250 hours](https://comforcarecareers.careerplug.com/jobs/2186144). The ComForCare link redirected when I opened it, so the posting may be closed.

## 3. What agencies pay today

- Home Care Pulse's 2022 study reported a median cost per caregiver acquired of [$561 via Indeed, $837 via referral programs and $167 via word of mouth](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2022/04/why-the-shifting-trends-in-home-care-recruitment-could-be-problematic/). The 2026 benchmark, as summarized by [HHAeXchange](https://www.hhaexchange.com/blog/reduce-aide-turnover-in-3-steps), puts word of mouth at $563. A $900 retained-aide fee is a premium over the average source.
- Boostpoint's vendor arithmetic puts ad-only cost per hire at [$34.70 to $173.50, or $104.10 at a 1-in-30 screening ratio](https://boostpoint.com/industries-healthcare/caregiver-staffing-agency-cost/).
- Larger skilled agencies pay more. HCS reports [average home care aide sign-on bonuses of $2,304 in 2025](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2025/11/home-health-worker-retention-improves-as-wages-bonuses-increase-in-2025/).
- The value of a retained aide is large. Florida aide services bill at a [median of about $68,640 a year at 44 hours a week](https://businesswire.com/news/home/20250301664457/en/Long-Term-Care-Costs-Increase-in-Florida-On-Par-with-National-Costs/), or about $30 an hour. The [Miami metro median wage is $15.81](https://wagedex.com/jobs/home-health-and-personal-care-aides/metro/miami-fort-lauderdale-west-palm-beach-fl). My estimate is a first-year gross spread of about $16K for a 25-hour-a-week aide, using an assumed 10% payroll burden. That makes $900 about 5% of one aide's first-year gross spread (inference).
- Demand is unmet. [63.3% of providers turned down cases in 2023 because of hiring shortfalls](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2024/08/caregiver-turnover-referral-rejections-continue-to-increase-in-home-care/), and only 12.8% of home care applicants were hired.
- I found no owner forum posts on willingness to pay for pay-on-retention pricing. That is a gap.

## 4. The retention problem, and the gate's number needs a caveat

- Turnover by an agency's top source (Activated Insights 2026, [via HHAeXchange](https://www.hhaexchange.com/blog/reduce-aide-turnover-in-3-steps)): own website 65.8%, employee referral 76.7%, word of mouth 77.1%, social media 107.0%.
- **Caveat on the 107%.** This compares agencies by their top source. It is not a survival curve for a candidate from that source, and it is confounded by pay. [Median turnover is 84.4% at $15 to $17.99 an hour and 53.0% at $18 to $19.99](https://hhaexchange.com/blog/recruiting-and-retaining-caregivers). I could not open the primary report. Social-heavy agencies are probably also low-wage (inference). The number is a warning, not proof.
- The older 2022 study found the reverse ordering: [word of mouth had 23.4% turnover and Indeed 84.5%](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2022/04/why-the-shifting-trends-in-home-care-recruitment-could-be-problematic/). Different years and methods, so the channel evidence is unstable.
- The first-90-days share is poorly sourced. Figures range from [more than 25% to 57% to over 80%](https://www.homecarepulse.com/articles/the-5-most-preventable-causes-of-90-day-caregiver-turnover/), and I could not trace any to a methodology.
- The type of agency matters. Skilled-agency aide turnover in HCS data is [34.17%](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2025/11/home-health-worker-retention-improves-as-wages-bonuses-increase-in-2025/), against [79.2% for home-based care](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2024/08/caregiver-turnover-referral-rejections-continue-to-increase-in-home-care/). The two surveys do not map cleanly onto each other. If MHC is a Medicare-certified skilled agency, its aide-retention pain may be much smaller, and it is a weak proof-of-need pilot (inference). The better targets are non-medical and licensed-only agencies.

## 5. Legal, licensing and platform issues

- **Immigration.** Federal law bars [recruiting or referring for a fee someone known to be unauthorized](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324a), with a good-faith verification defense. The DOJ civil-rights office pursues staffing firms for document demands (see its [FY2024 letters](https://www.justice.gov/crt/ier-letters-resolutions-fy-2024)). I could not find the specific recruiter-for-a-fee case the gate cited. Rule: the agency runs I-9 and E-Verify, and the network never asks for a particular document. Florida requires [E-Verify at 25 or more employees](https://gunster.com/alerts/fl-bill-1718-mandates-e-verify-for-all-florida-employers-with-25-or-more-employees). The 2026 bill to extend it to all employers [died in the Senate](https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026/197/ByVersion). Budget the $500 to $1,000 lawyer review.
- **Licenses.** Placing W-2 aides needs no state license I could find. A secondary source says [Florida has no state employment-agency license](https://www.harborcompliance.com/florida-employment-agency-peo-talent-license). Chapter 449, which the gate flagged, does not appear in the 2025 chapter list. I did not find the answer in the statutes themselves, so counsel should confirm.
- **Two traps.** Referring independent contractors to private homes is a [nurse registry, which needs an AHCA license](https://m.flsenate.gov/Statutes/400.506). Supplying temporary aides to agencies is a [health care services pool, which needs AHCA registration](https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2025/400.980). That blocks the "Surge Bench" extension.
- **Patient brokering.** Florida makes it a [third-degree felony or worse](https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2025/817.505) to pay anything for patient or business referrals. Referral rewards to churches, radio hosts or aides must be for candidates only, never clients. I did not research the federal Anti-Kickback Statute.
- **Platforms.** Meta requires [employment ads to declare the Special Ad Category and disables age, gender and zip targeting](https://www.jonloomer.com/special-ad-categories-meta-ads/). WhatsApp requires [opt-in before messaging](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/getting-opt-in), so cold group scraping is out.
- **Age.** Asher is 18, so B2B contracts are not a blocker. HIPAA is mostly avoided because recruiting data is HR data (inference).

## 6. First customers and how to reach them

- **MHC is unverified.** I found no public record tying "MHC Healthcare" to Florida home health. The nearest hit, [mhcorp.com](https://mhcorp.com/about), is a clinic group in other states. Ask the family for the legal entity, services (skilled or non-medical) and annual aide hires before building anything.
- **The association.** The Home Care Association of Florida lists [6,056 in-home care providers: 2,305 home health agencies (1,154 licensed-only, 1,151 Medicare/Medicaid-certified) and 1,197 nurse registries](https://homecareassociationoffloridainc.growthzoneapp.com/ap/CloudFile/Download/pjM2N8gr). Its vendor guide lists [HomeCareCon sponsor fees of $5,000 to $15,000, exhibit fees of about $1,150, and $1,000 to $5,000 for the winter Warm Up](https://growthzonesitesprod.azureedge.net/wp-content/uploads/sites/2156/2024/01/HCAF-2024-Marketing-Guide.pdf). Its [events calendar](https://homecareassociationoffloridainc.growthzoneapp.com/events) showed the 2025 Private Care Symposium in October and the 2026 Warm Up in January. I found no 2027 dates.
- **Targets.** Licensed-only agencies and nurse registries are the pain. Examples with live bilingual postings: [Matrix Home Care](https://www.careerbuilder.com/job-details/bilingual-english-spanish-certified-nursing-assistant-cna-home-health-aide-hha-miami-fl-33125-33145-33133-area-miami-fl--eede42c2-5e2a-4a68-8a38-da387ae808ce) (Spanish preferred, $18 to $21 an hour), [BrightStar North Miami](https://careers.brightstarcare.com/job-detail-179895885-home-health-aide-hha-spanish-speaking-weekend-availably-required/) (Spanish-speaking HHA postings) and The Lakes Home Care (Creole-speaking HHA postings, per the gate report).
- **Supply.** FVI, FMU and workforce boards (above). The [Haiti TPS ruling](https://www.wlrn.org/light/immigration/2026-07-06/politifact-fl-will-the-end-of-temporary-protected-status-for-haitians-mean-a-caregiving-crisis) hit a community of about 158,000 Haitian TPS holders in Florida. Sources conflict on the end date (July 10, July 27 to 30, and an earlier February notice). The supply shrank, but it is also the pool most afraid of outreach.

## 7. Unit economics and size

Model: $300 at start, $600 at day 90, one free replacement (no new start fee, day-90 fee if the replacement survives). All figures are my arithmetic.

| Day-90 survival | Sourcing cost per start | Revenue per slot | Gross margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| 40% | $250 / $400 | $684 | 42% / 6% |
| 50% | $250 / $400 | $750 | 50% / 20% |
| 65% | $250 / $400 | $826 | 59% / 35% |

- Survival is everything. Below 50% with $400 starts, there is no business. The $250 to $400 cost is an assumption: the ads are cheap ($104 to $188 per hire), while screening, a paid Creole-speaking community recruiter, referral rewards and check-in labor are not.
- **Market.** [Florida has about 90,170 aides](https://wagedex.com/jobs/home-health-and-personal-care-aides/florida) (BLS OEWS May 2025), and the Miami metro about 28,350. At 75% turnover that is about 21,000 replacement hires a year, or about $19M at $900. A 10% share is about $1.9M gross, or about $1.5M after an assumed 20% haircut for missed targets and replacements, close to the gate's $1.2M median.
- **Nationally** the pool is large, but $10M means about 13,000 retained hires a year at about $750 of revenue per slot. That needs multi-metro operations and community recruiters in each language. Venture-scale analogs are software: [Incredible Health reached a $1.65B valuation](https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/digital-health/incredible-health-reaches-1-65b-valuation/) selling nurse hiring to hospitals, and Carefam raised $14.5M. Neither is a $900-per-aide fee business.

## 8. Why now, and what cuts both ways

- **Tailwinds.** Authorized-worker supply shrank. Honor's CEO says ["we are, right now, today, short care pros"](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2026/08/staffing-gaps-turned-away-referrals-the-cost-of-ending-tps-for-haitian-home-care-workers/). [Immigrants are 46% of Florida's direct care workforce](https://www.phinational.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/PHI-Policy-Brief-Support-Immigrants-June-24-2026.pdf). Florida's minimum wage [rose to $15 on 30 Sep 2026](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/29/floridas-minimum-wage-increases-to-15-on-wednesday/), squeezing agency margins and raising the value of keeping each hire.
- **Headwinds.** AI voice recruiters and funded hiring platforms are commoditizing top-of-funnel screening. The shrinking pool lowers survival in the very channel Asher sells. Medicaid pressure may shrink the agencies' budgets (not researched).

## 9. Restructured offer (without shrinking the market)

1. **Concierge first.** Sell a bilingual new-hire retention line (Creole, Spanish, English check-ins at days 3, 14, 30 and 60 with escalation to the agency) to agencies' own hires. Proposed price: $500 to $900 a month per agency or about $200 per onboarded aide. The price comes from the benchmarks above (Carework from $720/mo, Home Care Marketing from $997/mo, replacement cost cited at [$2,600 per caregiver](https://enginehire.io/caregiver-retention-and-turnover-for-home-care-2026/)). This tests whether anyone pays for retention before taking sourcing risk.
2. **Placement second,** from schools and workforce boards, at $300 and $600 with hour minimums and payroll proof in the contract.
3. **Data third.** Survival curves by channel and agency. Peers will pay for evidence, not for a teenager's pitch.

## 10. 60-day test and kill criteria

- Weeks 1-2: confirm MHC's entity, services and aide hires; lawyer review; draft a two-page pilot agreement.
- Weeks 3-8: a pilot of 10 to 20 starts, tracking survival at days 14, 30 and 90. Take five owner meetings through the grandfather and the association.
- **Kill** if day-30 survival is under 70%, cost per start is over $400, or fewer than three non-family agencies sign a paid pilot within 90 days.

## 11. Gaps

- MHC's identity, type and aide volume.
- The primary Activated Insights 2026 report (I used HHAeXchange's summary).
- Any Florida-specific aide turnover (the HCAF report is paid).
- Pool size of Creole-speaking workers by county.
- Whether CareerSource funds aide roles.
- Owner willingness-to-pay posts.
- Statutory confirmation on Chapter 449 and employment-agency licensing.

On the buyer side, QAPIplus (a home-health compliance-software vendor) publishes an eight-area AI vendor evaluation checklist and webinars, and Apricot and Enzo publish 'questions to ask AI vendors' content. A $2,500-$5,000 bake-off has to beat free plus 'do it ourselves.'

Vendors cite 'internal audits' and self-reported accuracy (Olli 98%+, CarePilot 98%, Copper 95%+), and a QAPIplus webinar summary has Olli saying it works with third-party organizations to validate its claims, so validation is vendor-selected and unpublished. Vendors want a badge, not an honest score, and the closest precedent (CHAI assurance labs) stalled partly on who pays. Agencies have no compliance mandate to buy: CMS keeps coding responsibility with the assessing clinician and treats external reviewers as advisory. The existing budget line is human OASIS/coding review ($40-70 per chart), and sellers such as SimiTree, Gateway/Axxess, Home Care Answers and Olli already own it and bundle AI checking into it. The agency buyer purchases a cleaner claim, not a vendor accuracy score. A bake-off is also one-time spend with no repeat evidence.

Workflow owners bundle the capability, so it becomes a feature rather than a service. Axxess ships an AI OASIS Scrubber inside its EHR. Brellium sells AI audit of 100% of notes. SimiTree is positioning its coders as the human auditors of AI coding (a September 24, 2026 'Audit Your AI' webinar). Olli sells AI plus certified coders at half the price of human-only review. Once the EHR or the coding vendor includes QA, a standalone eval is redundant. The 'AI grading AI' layer is a product feature, not a gap.

The gap is real but is a public-goods gap, so the fix gets published free and ends the business. GAO (July 2026) flagged 'few independent studies' of AI coding and documentation accuracy. That invites academic, CMS, URAC, CHAI and Vals work, which would be free or bundled. A 'first to a standard' story needs years of vendor trust and legal capital, and the slots are filling (URAC accreditation, Vals neutral benchmarks, Qualified Health assurance, Onboard AI vendor vetting). The bench is not a moat either: his experts can earn more at Mercor directly, and Mercor's own episode (cutting thousands of contractors, then re-offering the work at about $5/hr less) shows how unstable expert supply economics are.

Commoditization is already underway on the demand side. Practitioner sources say teams build domain eval sets in-house ('buy breadth, build depth') and use LLM judges for volume, keeping humans for 5-10% calibration spot-checks. That shrinks expert-hours per customer. The sophisticated buyers who could pay can build, and the unsophisticated ones want finished solutions rather than evals. An essay on why independent eval startups fail argues the market is small and the best talent and revenue go to post-training or tooling. A March 2026 forum thread (low-quality source) reports 4 eval startups acquired in 5 months. He would be a family-affiliated 18-year-old grading vendors that sell to, or may be, his family's company.
